At 873 K and 10 s residence time, simulations predicted ~73 wt% olefins and ~21 wt% paraffins, in close agreement with experimental values of ~69 wt% and ~22 wt%, respectively. In contrast, hydrogen formation was substantially overpredicted (5.5 wt% versus 0.3 wt% experimentally), while dienes (0.3 wt% versus 6.4 wt%) and aromatics (0 wt% versus 1.6 wt%) were underpredicted. At higher temperature (923K), hydrogen overprediction intensified (9.6 wt% simulated versus 0.3 wt% experimental), although agreement for olefin carbon-number distributions improved at select residence time (10s). These comparisons provided clear quantitative diagnostics of where reaction thermochemistry requires targeted improvement. Beyond product-class yields, the work resolved carbon-number–specific biases that explain systematic distortions in predicted product slates. At 873 K and 10 s residence time, ethylene, propylene, and butene matched with experimental observation, while larger olefins such as pentene and heptene were underpredicted. This imbalance was traced to the absence of internal olefin formation pathways in existing reaction libraries, which favor terminal β-scission routes and concentrate flux into small olefins. To address this limitation, density functional theory calculations were used to identify and parameterize previously missing or poorly described elementary steps, including hydrogen abstraction and cyclic mechanisms responsible for internal olefin formation. For representative pathways leading to 2-pentene, computed activation barriers demonstrated that these mechanisms are kinetically accessible under pyrolysis conditions and competitive with β-scission, providing a mechanistic basis for improving higher-carbon olefin yields. Molecular structure as captured by branch size and branch density were further shown to exert a strong influence on backbone C–C dissociation kinetics in polyolefins. First- principles calculations revealed a clear trend in backbone C–C dissociation barriers: HDPE (365.4 kJ/mol) PP (321.3 kJ/mol) > LDPE (308.3 kJ/mol). Analysis of competing bond-breaking pathways showed that side-chain cleavage becomes kinetically preferred only when branch size≫ exceeds C . In polypropylene (PP) plastics, the methyl branch is 2 too small to decompose prior to backbone scission, and backbone C–C bond breaking therefore precedes C(backbone)–CH cleavage. Despite lower backbone scission barriers, PP does not generate higher yields of light gas-phase products. Owing to its high –CH branch density, polypropylene s₃uppresses the formation of light gases (n < 4), C producing only ~75% of the gas products formed from HDPE for chains of identical mole₃cular size, consistent with experimental observations. The importance of accurate mechanistic representation is reinforced by recent theory– experiment integration reported in our work (Li et al., 2023b), which demonstrated that polyolefin pyrolysis proceeds primarily through free-radical C–C scission followed by hydrogen abstraction. This work identified a key hydrogen-transfer step with ΔG‡ ≈ 119 kJ/mol and an overall exergonicity of −48.8 kJ/mol for paraffin–olefin formation and showed that diene formation is characterized by higher transition-state energy (~364 kJ/mol) than paraffin–olefin channels (~353 kJ/mol), explaining the experimentally observed suppression of diene yields.
